outline.chapter_title: Domestic Violence Call and On-Scene Facts
outline.description: Reconstructs the events at the Coleman residence using the body camera footage, highlighting the dialogue that the court viewed as supplying consent and the ensuing welfare check that led to a warrant and the discovery of firearms.
subtopics: 911 call reporting threats by Jaison Coleman against Lisa Coleman at 4:00 a.m.
Officer Kizer’s initial contact with Lisa on the porch and her hesitancy about the children’s safety
First request to enter and Lisa’s initial refusal
Lisa going back inside; officer’s limited door crack and welfare inquiries
The pivotal exchange: officer’s statement about ‘need’ to enter; Lisa’s ‘Okay’ and guidance on kids and dogs
Lisa opening the door and facilitating entry; pointing out bedrooms
Locating Coleman; protective pat down; children’s statements about threats and a gun
Transition from welfare check to warrant: securing a search warrant and finding several guns

outline.chapter_title: Procedural History and Issues on Appeal
outline.description: Tracks the case from indictment to appeal and sharpens the questions the Seventh Circuit resolved.
subtopics: Federal indictment under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) for felon-in-possession
Motion to suppress: argument that Lisa never consented and that officers exceeded any consent
Magistrate judge’s recommendation denying suppression; district court’s adoption
Conditional guilty plea preserving suppression challenge
Issues on appeal: (1) Was Lisa’s consent voluntary? (2) Did officers exceed the scope of consent?
Seventh Circuit’s reliance on body camera video to assess facts

outline.description: Sets out the legal standards the court applied for consent searches of homes, third-party consent, voluntariness, scope, and the lens of appellate review.
subtopics: Consent as a categorical exception to the warrant requirement (Schneckloth; Banks)
Third-party consent where shared privacy interests exist (Matlock; Cellitti)
Voluntariness requirement: ‘freely and voluntarily’ under totality of circumstances (Bumper; Han)
Common voluntariness factors (Figueroa-Espana; Santiago)
Scope of consent: objective reasonableness—what a typical person would understand (Jimeno; Saucedo; Jackson)
Appellate standard of review: clear error for voluntariness and scope findings (Jones)
Use of video evidence to resolve factual disputes (Scott v. Harris; Norville)

outline.chapter_title: Application: Voluntariness and Scope in a Welfare Check
outline.description: Explains how the Seventh Circuit applied the legal standards to the bodycam-recorded interaction, addressing the ‘need’ phrasing, Lisa’s demonstrated agency, and why the officers’ actions remained within the consent’s scope.
subtopics: Tone and demeanor: concern versus coercion; brief, calm interactions
Evidence of agency: Lisa’s initial refusal shows awareness and capacity to deny consent
Second request and response: ‘I’m sensing we almost need to come inside’ followed by Lisa’s ‘Okay’
Why ‘need’ did not render consent involuntary in context (Hicks; totality of circumstances)
Absence of custody, threats, or physical coercion; brief duration; implied awareness of choice
Post-consent conduct signaling understanding: directions about kids and dogs; opening door; facilitating entry
Scope analysis: reasonable understanding that consent was to check children’s welfare and ensure safety
Permissible actions within scope: scanning house, locating occupants, brief questioning, protective pat down
Causal chain to warrant: information gathered led to valid warrant; firearms recovered
No need to reach exigent circumstances or inevitable discovery given valid consent and scope

outline.description: States the court’s bottom line and distills lessons for practitioners about consent during domestic-violence welfare checks and the evidentiary role of video.
subtopics: Holding: No clear error in finding voluntary third-party consent; officers stayed within the scope
Disposition: Conviction affirmed; suppression properly denied
Significance for policing domestic violence calls: balanced approach to welfare concerns and consent
Importance of precise, non-coercive phrasing and calm demeanor in consent requests
Body camera footage as decisive evidence in consent and scope disputes
Practice pointers: articulating purpose of entry, confirming consent, limiting actions to stated objectives, transitioning to warrants when probable cause arises
